claim: Heterotopic ossification (HO) occurs following mechanical trauma and burns, or congenitally in patients suffering from fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP).
source: Heterotopic ossification (HO) occurs following mechanical trauma and burns, or congenitally in patients suffering from fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP).
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established medical knowledge about HO and FOP.

claim: Inhibitors of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase alpha (PI3Kα) may be a useful therapy for patients undergoing HO.
source: Recently, we demonstrated that inhibitors of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase alpha (PI3Kα) may be a useful therapy for patients undergoing HO.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: BYL719 effectively prevents HO even when administered up to 3–7 days after injury.
source: We found that BYL719 effectively prevents HO even when administered up to 3–7 days after injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1.

claim: The major actions of BYL719 are on-target effects through the inhibition of PI3Kα, without directly affecting ACVR1 or FOP-inducing ACVR1R206H kinase activities.
source: We demonstrate in cell cultures and in a mouse model of HO that the major actions of BYL719 are on-target effects through the inhibition of PI3Kα, without directly affecting ACVR1 or FOP-inducing ACVR1R206H kinase activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell culture and mouse models presented in the manuscript.

claim: A lack of PI3Kα in progenitors at injury sites is sufficient to prevent HO.
source: In vivo, we found that a lack of PI3Kα in progenitors at injury sites is sufficient to prevent HO.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experimental data using genetic models.

claim: BYL719 blocks osteochondroprogenitor specification.
source: Moreover, time course assays in HO lesions demonstrate that BYL719 not only blocks osteochondroprogenitor specification but also reduces the inflammatory response.
evidence: This claim is supported by time course experimental data in HO lesions.

claim: BYL719 reduces the inflammatory response in HO lesions.
source: Moreover, time course assays in HO lesions demonstrate that BYL719 not only blocks osteochondroprogenitor specification but also reduces the inflammatory response.
evidence: This claim is supported by time course experimental data in HO lesions.

claim: BYL719 inhibits the migration, proliferation, and expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in monocytes and mast cells.
source: BYL719 inhibits the migration, proliferation, and expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in monocytes and mast cells, suggesting that BYL719 hampers the hyper-inflammatory status of HO lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on cell migration, proliferation, and gene expression.

claim: PI3Kα inhibition is a safe and effective therapeutic strategy for HO.
source: Altogether, these results highlight the potential of PI3Kα inhibition as a safe and effective therapeutic strategy for HO.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Trauma-induced HO develops as a common post-operative complication after orthopedic surgeries (e.g. hip arthroplasty).
source: Trauma-induced HO develops as a common post-operative complication after orthopedic surgeries (e.g. hip arthroplasty).
evidence: This statement references established medical knowledge about HO.

claim: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is a rare congenital autosomal dominant disorder involving HO.
source: Blast gene-induced HO, fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is a rare congenital autosomal dominant disorder also involving HO (Bravenboer et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bravenboer et al., 2015.

claim: Ectopic bones form progressively through endochondral ossification, mostly in episodic flare-ups associated with inflammation.
source: Ectopic bones form progressively through endochondral ossification, mostly in episodic flare-ups associated with inflammation (Towler and Shore, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Towler and Shore, 2022.

claim: Cumulative osteogenic events lead to reduced mobility resulting from ankylosing joints.
source: These cumulative osteogenic events lead to reduced mobility resulting from ankylosing joints.
evidence: This statement describes a known consequence of HO based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Affected individuals have a shorter life span, most commonly due to thoracic insufficiency syndrome.
source: Affected individuals have a shorter life span, most commonly due to thoracic insufficiency syndrome (Kaplan et al., 2010; Pignolo et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kaplan et al., 2010 and Pignolo et al., 2016.

claim: HO reflects a shift from a normal tissue repair process to an aberrant reactivation of bone-forming developmental programs that require acute inflammation and the excessive expansion of local progenitors.
source: HO reflects a shift from a normal tissue repair process to an aberrant reactivation of bone-forming developmental programs that require acute inflammation and the excessive expansion of local progenitors, followed by inappropriate differentiation of these progenitors into chondroblasts and osteoblasts which finally results in bone formation (Hwang et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hwang et al., 2022.

claim: In both trauma-induced HO and FOP, pathology appears following the excessive activation of receptors sensitive to transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) superfamily members.
source: In both trauma-induced HO and FOP, pathology appears following the excessive activation of receptors sensitive to transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) superfamily members (Lees-Shepard et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lees-Shepard et al., 2018 and Wang et al., 2018.

claim: FOP arises from gain-of-function mutations in the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) type I receptor, encoded by the ACVR1 gene, with the most common mutation being c.617G>A, R206H.
source: FOP arises from gain-of-function mutations in the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) type I receptor, encoded by the ACVR1 gene, with the most common mutation being c.617G>A, R206H (Shore et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shore et al., 2006.

claim: Higher SMAD1/5-mediated signaling of mutated ACVR1 has been partially attributed to a loss of auto-inhibition of the receptor and mild hypersensitivity to BMP ligands.
source: Higher SMAD1/5-mediated signaling of mutated ACVR1 has been partially attributed to a loss of auto-inhibition of the receptor and mild hypersensitivity to BMP ligands (Chaikuad et al., 2012; Groppe et al., 2011; van Dinther et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chaikuad et al., 2012; Groppe et al., 2011; and van Dinther et al., 2010.

claim: Signaling by mutated ACVR1 still relies on ligand-induced heterotetrameric clustering but, unlike wild-type ACVR1, does not require ACVR2A/B kinase activity.
source: Signaling by mutated ACVR1 still relies on ligand-induced heterotetrameric clustering but, unlike wild-type ACVR1, does not require ACVR2A/B kinase activity (Agnew et al., 2021; Ramachandran et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Agnew et al., 2021 and Ramachandran et al., 2021.

claim: Mutated ACVR1 receptors alter their signaling specificity, abnormally activating SMAD1/5 and altering the non-canonical BMP signals (e.g. p38 or PI3K) in response to activin A.
source: More importantly, mutated ACVR1 receptors alter their signaling specificity, abnormally activating SMAD1/5 and altering the non-canonical BMP signals (e.g. p38 or PI3K) in response to activin A (Hatsell et al., 2015; Hino et al., 2015; Valer et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hatsell et al., 2015; Hino et al., 2015; and Valer et al., 2019.

claim: Activin A is necessary and sufficient for HO in FOP.
source: Accordingly, evidence supports that activin A is necessary and sufficient for HO in FOP (Hatsell et al., 2015; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018; Upadhyay et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hatsell et al., 2015; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018; and Upadhyay et al., 2017.

claim: Activin A does not drive post-traumatic HO.
source: In contrast, activin A does not drive post-traumatic HO (Hwang et al., 2020), and non-genetically driven HO mostly arises from excessive BMP and TGF-β signaling, with functional redundancy between different type I receptors of the TGF-β superfamily (Agarwal et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2022; Sorkin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hwang et al., 2020; Agarwal et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2022; Sorkin et al., 2020; and Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Non-genetically driven HO mostly arises from excessive BMP and TGF-β signaling, with functional redundancy between different type I receptors of the TGF-β superfamily.
source: In contrast, activin A does not drive post-traumatic HO (Hwang et al., 2020), and non-genetically driven HO mostly arises from excessive BMP and TGF-β signaling, with functional redundancy between different type I receptors of the TGF-β superfamily (Agarwal et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2022; Sorkin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Agarwal et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2022; Sorkin et al., 2020; and Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Mesenchymal fibroadipogenic precursors (FAPs) are the key cell-of-origin that aberrantly undergo chondrogenesis and further ectopic bone formation.
source: Evidence points to mesenchymal fibroadipogenic precursors (FAPs), which are widely distributed in muscle and other connective tissues, as the key cell-of-origin that aberrantly undergo chondrogenesis and further ectopic bone formation (Dey et al., 2016; Eisner et al., 2020; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dey et al., 2016; Eisner et al., 2020; and Lees-Shepard et al., 2018.

claim: Both FOP and non-genetic HO require local tissue destruction and inflammation, which indicate that FAPs should be invariably primed for ectopic bone formation by this inflammatory microenvironment.
source: However, both FOP and non-genetic HO also require local tissue destruction and inflammation, which indicate that FAPs should be invariably primed for ectopic bone formation by this inflammatory microenvironment (Barruet et al., 2018; Convente et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2022; Matsuo et al., 2019; Pignolo et al., 2013; Sorkin et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Barruet et al., 2018; Convente et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2022; Matsuo et al., 2019; Pignolo et al., 2013; and Sorkin et al., 2020.

claim: Inflammation in HO is characterized by an initial acute response following injury with the activation of innate immunity and the influx of neutrophils and monocytes.
source: Inflammation in HO is characterized by an initial acute response following injury with the activation of innate immunity and the influx of neutrophils and monocytes (Convente et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Convente et al., 2018 and Hwang et al., 2022.

claim: B and T cells of the adaptive system are also recruited in HO.
source: Additionally, B and T cells of the adaptive system are also recruited (Chakkalakal et al., 2012; Convente et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chakkalakal et al., 2012 and Convente et al., 2018.

claim: Mice lacking B or T lymphocytes exhibited no delay in the development of HO after injury, indicating that these cells may play a subsequent role in the dissemination of bone lesions.
source: However, mice lacking B or T lymphocytes exhibited no delay in the development of HO after injury, indicating that these cells may play a subsequent role in the dissemination of bone lesions (Kan et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kan et al., 2009 and includes an inference about the role of these cells.

claim: During intermediate and late inflammatory stages, the recruitment of monocytes, macrophages, and mast cells occurs, which in turn exerts autocrine and paracrine effects on nearby FAPs.
source: During intermediate and late inflammatory stages, the recruitment of monocytes, macrophages, and mast cells occurs, which in turn exerts autocrine and paracrine effects on nearby FAPs (Chakkalakal et al., 2012; Convente et al., 2018; Sorkin et al., 2020; Tu et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chakkalakal et al., 2012; Convente et al., 2018; Sorkin et al., 2020; and Tu et al., 2023.

claim: The depletion of mast cells and macrophages profoundly impairs genetic and non-genetic HO.
source: Highlighting their relevance in HO, the depletion of mast cells and macrophages profoundly impairs genetic and non-genetic HO (Convente et al., 2018; Torossian et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Convente et al., 2018; Torossian et al., 2017; and Tu et al., 2023.

claim: BMP receptors are robustly expressed in monocytes and macrophages.
source: BMP receptors are robustly expressed in monocytes and macrophages and the expression of ACVR1R206H has been shown to extend inflammatory responses in patient-derived macrophages (Barruet et al., 2018; Matsuo et al., 2021; Matsuo et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Barruet et al., 2018; Matsuo et al., 2021; and Matsuo et al., 2019.

claim: The expression of ACVR1R206H has been shown to extend inflammatory responses in patient-derived macrophages.
source: BMP receptors are robustly expressed in monocytes and macrophages and the expression of ACVR1R206H has been shown to extend inflammatory responses in patient-derived macrophages (Barruet et al., 2018; Matsuo et al., 2021; Matsuo et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Barruet et al., 2018; Matsuo et al., 2021; and Matsuo et al., 2019.

claim: Among the plethora of cytokines secreted by monocytes, macrophages, and mast cells, both activin A and TGF-β stand out as extremely relevant for HO.
source: Among the plethora of cytokines secreted by monocytes, macrophages, and mast cells, both activin A and TGF-β stand out as extremely relevant for HO (Alessi Wolken et al., 2018; Hatsell et al., 2015; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018; Patel et al., 2022; Sorkin et al., 2020; Upadhyay et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alessi Wolken et al., 2018; Hatsell et al., 2015; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018; Patel et al., 2022; Sorkin et al., 2020; and Upadhyay et al., 2017.

claim: Osteochondroprogenitor specification and maturation depend on phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase-α (PI3Kα).
source: Genetic and pharmacological studies have indicated that osteochondroprogenitor specification and maturation depend on phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase-α (PI3Kα) (Ford-Hutchinson et al., 2007; Fujita et al., 2004; Ikegami et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ford-Hutchinson et al., 2007; Fujita et al., 2004; and Ikegami et al., 2011.

claim: PI3K signaling is linked to HO, since inhibitors of PI3Kα (BYL719/Alpelisib/Piqray) prevented HO in mouse models without major side-effects.
source: We found that PI3K signaling was also linked to HO, since inhibitors of PI3Kα (BYL719/Alpelisib/Piqray) prevented HO in mouse models without major side-effects (Valer et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Valer et al., 2019.

claim: PI3Kα inhibitors hamper canonical and non-canonical BMP signaling, decreasing total and phosphorylated SMAD1/5 levels and reducing transcriptional responsiveness to BMPs/activin A in mesenchymal progenitors.
source: Mechanistically, PI3Kα inhibitors hamper canonical and non-canonical BMP signaling, decreasing total and phosphorylated SMAD1/5 levels and reducing transcriptional responsiveness to BMPs/activin A in mesenchymal progenitors (Gámez et al., 2016; Valer et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gámez et al., 2016 and Valer et al., 2019.

claim: The pharmacological and genetic inhibition of PI3Kα in HO progenitors at injury sites reduces HO in vivo.
source: In the current study, we demonstrate that the pharmacological and genetic inhibition of PI3Kα in HO progenitors at injury sites reduces HO in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The delayed administration of BYL719, up to 7 days after inflammatory injury, still prevents HO in mice.
source: Moreover, envisioning a future translation into the clinic, we have optimized the administration of BYL719 and found that the delayed administration of BYL719, up to 7 days after inflammatory injury, still prevents HO in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BYL719 effectively reduces the essential inflammatory response in HO.
source: In addition, we found that BYL719 blocks osteochondroprogenitor specification and effectively reduces the essential inflammatory response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The early administration of the treatment with BYL719 at day 1 or 3 after the onset of HO resulted in significantly lower HO.
source: The early administration of the treatment with BYL719 at day 1 or 3 after the onset of HO resulted in significantly lower HO; late administration 7 days after the induction of HO was also partially effective (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Late administration of BYL719 7 days after the induction of HO was partially effective.
source: The early administration of the treatment with BYL719 at day 1 or 3 after the onset of HO resulted in significantly lower HO; late administration 7 days after the induction of HO was also partially effective (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Discontinuation of the treatment after 3 days did not prevent HO at day 23.
source: Discontinuation of the treatment after 3 days did not prevent HO at day 23.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The inhibition of PI3Kα by BYL719 after injury prevents HO, and this protection is still effective if the treatment is started several days after injury, expanding its therapeutic window.
source: These results indicate that the inhibition of PI3Kα by BYL719 after injury prevents HO, and this protection is still effective if the treatment is started several days after injury, expanding its therapeutic window.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Genetic deletion of Pik3ca in mice expressing ACVR1Q207D led to a reduction in HO.
source: Genetic deletion of Pik3ca in mice expressing ACVR1Q207D led to a reduction in HO, which was further enhanced by BYL719 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The reduction in HO from genetic deletion of Pik3ca was further enhanced by BYL719.
source: Genetic deletion of Pik3ca in mice expressing ACVR1Q207D led to a reduction in HO, which was further enhanced by BYL719 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No significant changes in the weight of the mice were observed, confirming the absence of severe toxicity.
source: Importantly, no significant changes in the weight of the mice were observed, confirming the absence of severe toxicity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In PI3Kα deficient mice, ACVR1Q207D expression only led to minor ectopic calcifications that were already surrounded by fully regenerated muscle tissue on the 23rd day after injury.
source: However, in PI3Kα deficient mice, ACVR1Q207D expression only led to minor ectopic calcifications that were already surrounded by fully regenerated muscle tissue on the 23rd day after injury (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The abrogation of PI3Kα activity (either genetically or pharmacologically) in cells at injury sites is relevant for their inhibitory effects in HO.
source: These results demonstrate that the abrogation of PI3Kα activity (either genetically or pharmacologically) in cells at injury sites is relevant for their inhibitory effects in HO.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The effects of BYL719 might be attributed to the direct effects on progenitor cell expansion and chondroblast specification, as well as its possible ability to reduce the inflammatory response required for HO.
source: This might be attributed to the direct effects of BYL719 on progenitor cell expansion and chondroblast specification, as well as its possible ability to reduce the inflammatory response required for HO.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanisms of BYL719 action.

claim: The overexpression of Acvr1R206H increased basal and activin-dependent expression of canonical (Id1 and Sp7) and activin-dependent expression of non-canonical (Ptgs2) BMP target genes.
source: The overexpression of Acvr1R206H increased basal and activin-dependent expression of canonical (Id1 and Sp7) and activin-dependent expression of non-canonical (Ptgs2) BMP target genes (Figure 3C), known markers and drivers of osteochondrogenic differentiation (Nakashima et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and citations to Nakashima et al., 2002 and Wang et al., 2013.

claim: Both pharmacological and genetic inhibition of PI3Kα reduced canonical and non-canonical ACVR1R206H transcriptional responses induced by activin A.
source: Both pharmacological and genetic inhibition of PI3Kα reduced canonical and non-canonical ACVR1R206H transcriptional responses induced by activin A.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stimulation with activin A increased its own transcription (Inhba) in Acvr1R206H-transduced BM-MSCs, which was also inhibited by BYL719.
source: Of note, stimulation with activin A increased its own transcription (Inhba) in Acvr1R206H-transduced BM-MSCs, which was also inhibited by BYL719 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: BYL719 may prevent osteochondroprogenitor differentiation indirectly, via transcriptional inhibition of INHBA/activin A expression.
source: Therefore, BYL719 may also prevent osteochondroprogenitor differentiation indirectly, via transcriptional inhibition of INHBA/activin A expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The effects of BYL719 on ACVR1-downstream signaling are mainly on target, due to PI3Kα kinase inhibition.
source: These results demonstrate a direct effect of BYL719 on osteochondroprogenitor cells and suggest that the effects of BYL719 on ACVR1-downstream signaling are mainly on target, due to PI3Kα kinase inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Treatment with BYL719 reduced the number of PDGFRA+ cells throughout the ossification process.
source: More importantly, treatment with BYL719 reduced the number of PDGFRA+ cells throughout the ossification process.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: An increase in the diameter of myofibers was observed in animals treated with BYL719.
source: We also observed an increase in the diameter of myofibers in animals treated with BYL719 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and 1C.

claim: The results suggest improved muscle regeneration in animals treated with BYL719 compared to those undergoing HO.
source: These results suggest improved muscle regeneration in animals treated with BYL719 compared to those undergoing HO.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: 2-aminothiazole-derived PI3Kα inhibitors could also inhibit ACVR1 kinase activity.
source: It is known that 2-aminothiazole-derived PI3Kα inhibitors could also inhibit ACVR1 kinase activity (Jamieson et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jamieson et al., 2011.

claim: BYL719 incubated at 1 and 10 µM failed to significantly inhibit the acceptor emission of the BMP type I receptors ACVRL11, ACVR1, BMPR1A, ACVR1B, TGFBR1, and the mutant receptor ACVR1R206H.
source: BYL719 incubated at 1 and 10 µM failed to significantly inhibit the acceptor emission of the BMP type I receptors ACVRL11, ACVR1, BMPR1A, ACVR1B, TGFBR1, and the mutant receptor ACVR1R206H (Figure 4C), without significant changes in the protein levels of each receptor (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: BYL719 does not target the activity of the type II kinase receptors ACVR2A, ACVR2B, BMPR2, and TGFBR2.
source: In addition, we demonstrated that BYL719 does not target the activity of the type II kinase receptors ACVR2A, ACVR2B, BMPR2, and TGFBR2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BYL719 exhibited no major effects on ACVR1R206H activity up to 10 µM in in vitro kinase activity assays with recombinant ACVR1R206H.
source: We confirmed these results using in vitro kinase activity assays with recombinant ACVR1R206H. BYL719 exhibited no major effects on ACVR1R206H activity up to 10 µM (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: BYL719 does not directly target the activity of ACVR1 or related receptors.
source: Given that BYL719 does not directly target the activity of ACVR1 or related receptors, we established two in vitro models to further profile the main targeted pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Recombinant activin A was able to induce SMAD1/5 activation and the expression of ACVR1-downstream targets ID1 and ID3 in cells overexpressing ACVR1R206H.
source: In human MSCs (hMSCs) stably overexpressing ACVR1 or ACVR1R206H, recombinant activin A was able to induce SMAD1/5 activation and the expression of ACVR1-downstream targets ID1 and ID3 in cells overexpressing ACVR1R206H (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Coincubation with BYL719 (10 μM) completely inhibited the formation of a chondrogenic glycosaminoglycans-rich matrix in response to TGFβ1 plus activin A in the different cell types.
source: Coincubation with BYL719 (10 μM) completely inhibited the formation of a chondrogenic glycosaminoglycans-rich matrix in response to TGFβ1 plus activin A in the different cell types (Figure 5A, B) and partially abrogated the expression of the chondrogenic genes ACAN and MMP13 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, 5B, and 5C.

claim: Coincubation with BYL719 (10 μM) partially abrogated the expression of the chondrogenic genes ACAN and MMP13.
source: Coincubation with BYL719 (10 μM) completely inhibited the formation of a chondrogenic glycosaminoglycans-rich matrix in response to TGFβ1 plus activin A in the different cell types (Figure 5A, B) and partially abrogated the expression of the chondrogenic genes ACAN and MMP13 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Coincubation with BYL719 (10 μM) was able to repress activin A-induced alkaline phosphatase activity upon 7 and 11 days of culture.
source: Furthermore, in these cells, coincubation with BYL719 (10 μM) was able to repress activin A-induced alkaline phosphatase activity upon 7 and 11 days of culture, respectively (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: ACVR1R206H mutant cells display an enhanced chondrogenic response to activin A compared to wild-type cells.
source: ACVR1R206H mutant cells display an enhanced chondrogenic response to activin A compared to wild-type cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In both wild type and mutant MSCs, treatment with BYL719 decreased the expression of chondrogenic genes.
source: In both wild type and mutant MSCs, treatment with BYL719 decreased the expression of chondrogenic.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BYL719 could inhibit chondrogenic differentiation of human and murine MSCs irrespective of the expression of either wild type or mutant ACVR1.
source: These results confirmed that BYL719 could inhibit chondrogenic differentiation of human and murine MSCs irrespective of the expression of either wild type or mutant ACVR1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ossification (GO:0001503) and osteoblast differentiation (GO:0001649) were detected as two of the ten most significantly differentially regulated biological processes between ACVR1WT and ACVR1R206H conditions.
source: Consistent with our results on osteogenic progenitor cells, gene ontology analysis of differentially expressed genes between cells expressing ACVR1WT and ACVR1R206H resulted in the robust regulation of relevant biological processes. Ossification (GO:0001503) and osteoblast differentiation (GO:0001649) were detected as two of the ten most significantly differentially regulated biological processes between these conditions (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The addition of BYL719 (1 µM) resulted in a downregulation of ossification and osteoblast differentiation GO terms for all conditions except activin A stimulated ACVR1WT cells.
source: The addition of BYL719 (1 µM) resulted in a downregulation of these GO terms for all conditions except activin A stimulated ACVR1WT cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Several inflammatory cytokine genes (e.g. IL6 and IL15) and inflammatory signaling pathways (e.g. TNF and NF-κB), were downregulated by BYL719.
source: Moreover, several inflammatory cytokine genes (e.g. IL6 and IL15) and inflammatory signaling pathways (e.g. TNF and NF-κB), were downregulated by BYL719 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Part of the mechanism by which BYL719 prevents HO in vivo may be due to the modulation of inflammatory responses.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that, in addition to preventing the activation of osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiation pathways in progenitor cells, part of the mechanism by which BYL719 prevents HO in vivo may be due to the modulation of inflammatory responses.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data.

claim: Monocytes, macrophages, and mast cells increase in number 2–4 days after injury.
source: These cell populations are known to increase in number 2–4 days after injury (Convente et al., 2018; Sorkin et al., 2020), which coincides with the effects observed following early administration of BYL719.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Convente et al., 2018 and Sorkin et al., 2020.

claim: After 16 days, structures of mineralized bone became detectable in vehicle-treated mice.
source: After 16 days, structures of mineralized bone became detectable in vehicle-treated mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: The number of F4/80-positive monocytes/macrophages was high 2 days after injury and remained elevated in the HO lesions throughout the ossification process.
source: The number of F4/80-positive monocytes/macrophages was high 2 days after injury and remained elevated in the HO lesions throughout the ossification process (Figure 7B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: BYL719-treated animals showed an almost 50% reduction in the number of F4/80-positive cells at day 2 post-injury onwards.
source: BYL719-treated animals showed an almost 50% reduction in the number of F4/80-positive cells at day 2 post-injury onwards.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.
